projects.title: Neon Rush
projects.tagline: A three-lane endless runner for the browser, built small but structured like a production game.
summary: Neon Rush is my take on the endless runner: three lanes, a jump, a slide, three kinds of hazard, pickups with a combo multiplier, and a difficulty curve that speeds the run up without shrinking the time you have to react.

It is a small game on purpose. I used it to show how I set up a Unity project that is expected to grow: modules with enforced boundaries, rules that run without the engine, content as data, and one codebase for the browser, Windows and Android. It is still in development, and the browser build is the one being worked on.
highlights: The title screen is a camera shot. Press play and the camera swings round behind the runner as the run begins.
Keyboard, gamepad, mouse and touch, with on-screen hints that follow the devices in use.
Every screen works from keys or a gamepad, and the run pauses when the window loses focus.
A crash you can see: a flash, a camera shake, sparks, and a game-over screen that waits for it to play out.
Sound effects and two music loops that crossfade between the title and the run. The audio is placeholder for now.
Seeded runs and a saved best score.
architecture: Four layers, each its own assembly: App, Features, Shared and Core. A feature cannot reference another feature. They talk through messages and small interfaces, which is how sound, effects and the cameras were added without touching gameplay code.

Game rules and UI presenters are plain C# with no MonoBehaviour, so they are covered by EditMode tests, including tests that fail if a frame of gameplay allocates. One simulation loop ticks every system in a fixed order. What differs between platforms is data: an input profile and settings per platform family, with no platform checks in gameplay or UI code.
learned: Measure on the real thing. The score display built no strings and passed its allocation test, and still allocated about 360 bytes on every change once it was on screen, because UI Toolkit allocates whenever a label's text changes. It is now a row of reels that slide, and a test measures whole frames on the live HUD.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the game costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Cine Director
projects.tagline: First Light: a 78-second film shot with Cinemachine and cut on one Timeline, with notes on every shot.
projects.role: Solo: direction, code, set, sound, build
summary: First Light is a short film made entirely inside Unity. A maintenance robot wakes in a dead station, walks a corridor on emergency lighting, throws the lever that brings the power back, crosses a bridge in the open air and watches a beacon light as the sun comes up.

I made it to show camera work and sequencing the way I would do them in a shipped game: not a baked video, but data on a timeline, played by a small app you can pause, skip through by chapter and read. A bar above the picture names each shot, the technique behind it and the lens, as the camera goes live.
highlights: Twelve shots, twelve techniques: a dolly on a spline, a rack focus, a tracking shot, hand-held, over the shoulder, an insert, a cut on a signal, a static frame, an orbit, a crane, a dolly zoom and a pull-back.
Director's notes in the top bar, which you can switch off with N.
Five chapters. Skip between them or jump to any one from the pause panel; picture, lighting and sound are right on the next frame, forwards or backwards.
A robot that walks without a single animation clip: the gait is driven by distance travelled and the legs are solved with IK.
A score that follows the chapters and ten effects, all synthesised for the film and kept in step with the picture.
Keyboard, mouse or gamepad. Leaving the tab pauses the film.
architecture: One rule shaped the project: everything you see or hear is worked out from the film's current time, and nothing remembers the frame before. The walker, the lamps, the doors, the dawn, the cameras and the sound are each a small custom Timeline track over a component that applies what it is given. That is why a jump to any chapter needs no reset code.

Around the film is the same structure as my other projects: App, Features, Shared and a core package, each its own assembly, wired by dependency injection. The transport, the screens and the camera notes are plain C# classes covered by EditMode tests, and eight PlayMode tests run the whole app from its first scene.
learned: Look at the picture where it will be watched. My editor screenshots were rendered into an 8-bit target, which clamps the image before bloom runs, so bloom looked absent and I kept turning it up. The first browser build showed the real thing: a halo round every lamp.

A set made of 249 boxes cost 1,226 draw calls on the title card alone. Merging everything that never moves brought that to 461, in pieces kept small enough that each one is still lit by the lamps nearest to it.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the film costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Tactica AI
projects.tagline: Grid tactics against a hand-written behaviour tree that shows its reasoning for every move.
projects.role: Solo: design, code, AI, models, sound, build
summary: A small turn-based tactics game: three units a side on a six by six board with walls and cover. You can play Blue against the AI, or let it play both sides and watch.

The point of it is the panel on the right. Game AI is easy to fake, so I built an opponent you can check: every time one of its units decides, the panel lays out the whole decision. Each node of its behaviour tree with yes, no or never asked and the reason, then the options it weighed with the score written out term by term. It is the record the tree writes while it runs, not a description made up afterwards.
highlights: A behaviour tree I wrote by hand, with scoring at its leaves: the tree picks what kind of thing to do (finish a kill, fall back, strike, close in) and a weighted sum over the facts picks exactly where and to whom.
Three unit classes with three different trees: a brawler, a skirmisher that shoots from the safest spot it can find, and a medic that heals whoever is worst off.
A decision inspector with history. Step back through every decision of the match while it carries on.
A danger map you can switch on: how much the enemy could do to each cell next turn. It is the AI's own map, worked out for the unit about to move.
No dice anywhere. The same position always gives the same decision, and a match between the two AIs plays out move for move the same in the editor and in the browser.
Keyboard or mouse, with a layout for wide screens and one for a screen held upright.
architecture: The rules are a library with no engine in it: board, movement, line of fire, combat and turns, as plain C# that tests can play without starting Unity. There is one way to change a battle, which is to hand it an action and have the rules check it. A click and an AI decision go through the same call, so the AI cannot do anything a player could not.

Trees, unit classes and arenas are assets. A tree is a ScriptableObject with its nodes inside it; a new kind of unit is an asset with numbers, a model and a tree; an arena is six strings. Around that is the same structure as my other projects: App, Features, Shared and a core package, each its own assembly, wired by dependency injection.

What you see lags what is true, on purpose. The rules settle an action at once and the board plays it out from a queue, one step at a time. The AI waits for the board before its next step, which is why you can watch it think one unit at a time.
learned: Tests that put each shipped tree into a position drawn for one behaviour found a real flaw in the AI. A unit judged how dangerous a cell was with itself still standing where it was, so in a corridor it fell back one cell to a spot the enemy could still reach. With that fixed, a match between the two AIs went from five turns to ten.

The first browser build made about 400 draw calls for six units. Every model was ten primitives, each drawn for colour, again for ambient occlusion and again for four shadow cascades. Merging each model into one mesh per material and cutting the render pipeline down to what a small board needs brought a match to between 85 and 137.

The first match began with a frame of nearly a second, because everything was drawn for the first time on the frame after Play was pressed. The board now draws itself once while the app starts, behind a cover, and the first match's longest frame is 12.5 ms.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the game costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Plane Simulation
projects.tagline: Take off, fly the circuit and land a jet on a flight model written from scratch, then read a debrief that grades the flight like a check ride.
projects.role: Solo: design, code, flight model, UI, sound, build
summary: One jet, one airfield. You start lined up on runway 36: open the throttle, rotate at the right speed, clean the aircraft up, fly round, select landing mode, follow the needles down and stop on the centreline. Then the game tells you how you did, item by item. It plays from the keyboard or a gamepad: W S A D for the stick, Left Shift and Left Ctrl for the throttle, G for the gear, F and V for the flaps, L for landing mode, M to turn the sound off.

I built it to do a simulation properly at a small scale. The aircraft is not a Unity rigid body with forces bolted on. It is my own six-degree-of-freedom model, stepped at a fixed 120 Hz, with lift that stalls, drag that changes near the ground, three sprung wheels and a fly-by-wire control law. It can be crashed, and the debrief will say why.
highlights: A flight model of my own, with no PhysX in it: a rigid body with six degrees of freedom, integrated at a fixed 120 Hz whatever the frame rate, with the drawn pose interpolated between steps.

Fly-by-wire. The stick asks for a pitch rate and a roll rate, and the control law protects the angle-of-attack and load-factor limits. Its authority comes from the airspeed, so the nose will not come up before rotation speed.

A check ride, not a score. The take-off is rated on six items and the landing on eleven, from centreline tracking and lift-off speed to sink rate, touchdown point, crab and bounces. Each is rated from Excellent to Fail against a band, and any Fail fails the ride.

Ways to crash: any part of the hull but the tail touching a surface, a touchdown that is too hard or too far sideways, an over-compressed strut, or running onto the grass too fast. The hangars and the tower are solid.
Approach guidance: needles for the glide slope and the centreline, the distance to the threshold and your speed against the reference, with PAPI lights beside the runway showing the same slope.

Sound made by code. The engine is a turbine whine with a roar that comes in with thrust, and with it the airflow, the wheels on the runway, the gear and flap motor, the stall warning, the touchdown and the crash. Every sound is synthesised from sines and filtered noise while the game loads: there are no audio files, and it added 0.06 MB to the download.
A scripted pilot in the tests flies the whole circuit through the real flight model, airfield and mission, from take-off to a full stop.
architecture: Because the aircraft owns its physics, it behaves the same on every platform and needs no scene. The tests fly it directly: several minutes of flight across the suite, in about a fifth of a second. Devices become a plain frame of actions before the game sees them, and the scripted pilot flies through exactly that seam.

Four layers, each its own assembly: App, Features, Shared and a small core. The seven features (input, flight, mission, world, HUD, camera, sound) never reference each other, so one reaching into another does not compile. They talk through messages and interfaces in Shared. Nothing in the project has an Update: everything that runs per frame is a plain class ticked in a fixed order.

Tuning is data. The aircraft, the airfield, the grading standards and the cameras are ScriptableObjects, and the scenes, prefabs, materials and input actions are built by an editor script. A validator fails that build if any reference is left empty.
learned: The first version of the sound shipped as audio files, and measuring the browser build showed two things I would not have heard for certain. Every loop came back from the browser about 20 ms longer than it went in, because Unity hands a browser compressed audio whatever the import settings say: a gap every time round. And a loop started at a pitch other than 1 played at the wrong pitch until its pitch next changed. The sounds are now rendered as samples when the game starts, at 44.1 kHz, and both are gone: each loop is exactly its length, and the flap motor measures 225 Hz where it should be 225.

The runway, its markings and the ground around it are one mesh in which no two faces overlap, so nothing flickers at any distance. That mesh could not be marked static: Unity's static batching drew it with the wrong sub-meshes.

A model can come back from a re-export with a control reversed and nobody notices until the aircraft rolls the wrong way. The content builder checks which way the jet faces and works out the deflection direction of every control surface by probing its hinge.

There is a lot it does not have yet: one aircraft, one runway, no wind. The sound is a first pass that I have measured more than I have tuned. The Android build has never been on a device, and nobody has landed the browser build by hand. The scripted pilot lands it in the tests.
The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what the game costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured yet.

projects.title: Rig Studio
projects.tagline: A rigged character with every layer on a switch: head look, foot planting, hand reach and a breathing constraint of my own.
projects.role: Solo: design, code, rigging, character, animation, sound, build
summary: A small robot stands on a turntable in a room. Three clips, idle, walk and run, play through one blend tree. Everything else it does is solved live on top of them: the head follows your pointer, the feet find the steps, the ramp and the bumps as the ground turns under them, the right hand reaches for an orb when it drifts into range, and the body breathes and shifts its weight.

Each of those is a rig layer with a switch, a weight slider and a solo button. Rigging is easy to take on trust, so I built it to be checked: turn a layer off and you see exactly what it was doing. A guided tour does that for you, one layer at a time, and a button draws the bones, the IK targets and the line of sight over the character.
highlights: Head look: three Multi-Aim constraints share the turn between chest, neck and head. It follows the pointer, watches the orb when the pointer rests, and faces forward again when asked to look behind itself.

Foot planting: Two-Bone IK on each leg. The ground is a height function, not colliders, so a foot knows the height of the step it will land on before it gets there, and the body rides at the height of the lower foot.
Hand reach: Two-Bone IK on the right arm, eased in as the orb comes into range, with the fingertips stopping at its surface.
Idle motion: a constraint of my own with its own animation job. Breath and a slow drift of weight, from noise, laid over the pose inside the animation stream.
A face of ten blend shapes on one mood slider, from angry to delighted, with procedural blinking over the top.

No art was downloaded. The skeleton, the skinned mesh, the blend shapes, the clips and the blend tree are generated by a tool I wrote, and the turntable is drawn from the same height function the feet are planted from.
Mouse, keyboard, gamepad and touch, with a layout for wide screens and one for a screen held upright. Every sound is synthesised when the app starts.
architecture: The rules are plain C# that never touches a bone: a gait model, a foot planter, a look model, a reach model, an idle model, an expression ramp. Each works out numbers, and a thin view copies them onto the rig. That is what lets 254 tests check foot placement, reach and look without a scene, and it is why none of it depends on frame timing.

The blend tree does not run by itself. Its time is a parameter the gait model drives, and the clips were baked from the same foot-path function the model evaluates at run time. So the rig knows where the animation is putting a foot this frame before the Animator has run, and IK is never a frame behind.

Around that is the same structure as my other projects: App, Features, Shared and a core package, each its own assembly, wired by dependency injection and ticked in one fixed order. Eight features, none of which references another.
learned: I did not know whether Animation Rigging runs in a browser, and the project stands on it. So as soon as the first constraints worked I made a throwaway build of two characters and nothing else. It does, custom job included: the head aimed within a degree of its target and the wrist landed within two millimetres of its own.
An animation job cannot call ordinary code, so my constraint is split in two. A plain class works out breath and sway, which is the part worth testing, and the job only applies what it is handed.

My first walk looked like a crouch. I had kept the legs to 96.5% of their length to leave room for the IK; at 98.5% it reads as a walk, and the rule that lowers the body to the lower foot gives the IK its room instead.

The numbers above come from a fast desktop and a local server. They show what a frame costs, not how it runs on a slow laptop or a phone, which I have not measured. And nobody has listened to the sound yet: I checked its levels and timing, not how it sounds.

projects.title: DevKit Pro
projects.tagline: Four Unity editor tools I kept rewriting, as one package that installs by Git URL and also runs from the command line.
summary: Every project of mine ended up with the same handful of editor scripts: something to find broken references before a build did, something to make every platform's build the same way twice, something to tell me what was really in the Addressables groups. DevKit Pro is those tools written once, properly, as a Unity package: a Scene and Asset Validator, a Build Runner, an Addressables Audit and a ScriptableObject Browser.

Each one is a window in the editor and also a command. The command writes a report, as JSON or as text, and ends with an exit code, so the check I run by hand is the same check a build script can fail on.

To install it, open the Package Manager, choose "Add package from git URL" and paste https://github.com/roadandcode/devkit-pro.git?path=Packages/com.roadandcode.devkit#v0.1.0 or download the .unitypackage above and import it. It needs Unity 6000.5 and nothing else. The Addressables Audit switches itself on when Addressables is installed.
highlights: Scene and Asset Validator: missing scripts, missing references, missing prefabs, reference fields left empty on the project's own scripts, and empty objects, across scenes, prefabs, ScriptableObjects and materials. Scenes that are not open are read and closed again without disturbing the ones that are.
Addressables Audit: groups nothing references, AssetReferences that lead nowhere, assets copied into several bundles because two groups need them, bundles over a size limit, and addresses used twice.

Build Runner: a Build Plan asset lists the project's Web, Windows and Android builds with an output path each. The plan is checked before anything is built, and player settings a build overrides are put back afterwards.
ScriptableObject Browser: every data asset in the project by type, with search and the inspector in place.
A preferences page per tool, and shortcuts registered with Unity's Shortcut Manager so they can be rebound.
No dependencies. It does not need my other packages or a dependency injection container, and it compiles in a project without Addressables.
architecture: One assembly per tool, all editor-only, and no tool references another. Inside a tool the analysis is plain C#: project data comes in as records, findings come out as data, and nothing in it touches the editor. Adapters read the project through the editor API, and a UI Toolkit window sits on top as a thin view over a presenter. Editor windows cannot be opened in an automated run, so everything a window does apart from drawing lives where a test can drive it.

The Addressables Audit is two assemblies. The rules know nothing about the Addressables package; a second assembly, compiled only when that package is present, reads its settings into the audit's own records. That is why the package installs cleanly into a project without Addressables, and why the rules can be tested there.

The two timings above are from my own projects, Tactica AI and Plane Simulation, with the package installed by Git URL into a copy of each. It found the same thing in both: nine components in the default volume profile, left there by Unity's project template, made from scripts that are in no project. It also showed me two things the validator had wrong, which sample data never would have.
learned: A build can report success and be broken. My first web build from the Build Runner finished with the right size and a success message, and had an Addressables catalog with no bundles behind it. Unity will build a platform the editor is not switched to, and Addressables will not follow. I only saw it because I opened the output folder. The tool switches platform first now.

Addressables tidies up after you without saying so. I planted an entry for a deleted asset to test a check, and it was gone the next time the project opened. No error, no failed build. What stays broken is the reference that pointed at it, so that is what the audit reports.
